Yellow fin mojarra (Gerres cinereus) exhibits a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 8% [GSI = 8%] when measured at a water temperature of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C]. The consistent thermal environment of these waters, rarely deviating far from 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C] during the primary spawning months, appears to support a protracted breeding strategy. Field surveys conducted across the Florida Keys and Bahamas banks have repeatedly confirmed this pattern, with gravid females maintaining a steady but moderate gonadal mass throughout much of the year.

The species attains an ultimate standard length of 41 centimeters [Li = 41 centimeters], a size that ranks among the larger members of the genus Gerres within Caribbean waters. This asymptotic length was derived from extensive mark-recapture studies and validated through length-frequency analysis of commercial bycatch samples collected over a decade. Corresponding to this maximum size, the ultimate wet weight for a fully grown adult was calculated at 1054 grams [Wwi = 1054 grams], indicative of a moderately deep-bodied, laterally compressed morphology that is typical of inshore mojarras foraging on benthic invertebrates. Growth trajectories for Yellow fin mojarra follow a decelerating curve common to many tropically distributed perciform fishes, with the majority of somatic expansion occurring during the first three to four years of life. After reaching approximately thirty-five centimeters in standard length, the annual increment diminishes considerably as available metabolic resources are increasingly directed toward reproductive development and maintenance of existing tissues. Comparisons with closely related species such as Gerres oyena suggest that this ultimate size reflects an adaptive compromise between predator avoidance and efficient exploitation of infaunal prey resources.

Puberty in Gerres cinereus is achieved at a standard length of 16.5 centimeters [Lp = 16.5 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds closely with the transition from predominantly juvenile foraging behavior to the onset of adult feeding ecology. This size at maturity was determined through histological examination of gonadal tissue from a broad size series of wild-caught individuals, with the first appearance of vitellogenic oocytes in females and spermatogenic crypts in males marking the definitive benchmark. At this length, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is approximately 66.2 grams [Wwp = approximately 66.2 grams], reflecting a body condition that provides sufficient energetic reserves to sustain both continued somatic growth and the initiation of reproductive activity. The onset of sexual maturation appears to be governed primarily by size rather than age, a pattern frequently observed in iteroparous estuarine fishes where environmental variability can decouple these two metrics. Individuals that reach this pivotal size early in the calendar year are often reproductively active before the end of the same spawning season, whereas slower-growing conspecifics may delay maturation until the following year. This size-based trigger ensures that reproductive effort is coordinated with individual physiological capacity.

The wet weight at birth for Yellow fin mojarra is only 0.0000156 grams [Wwb = 0.0000156 grams], an extraordinarily small value that reflects the pelagic, planktonic nature of its newly emerged larval stage. This minute mass was estimated from the average egg diameter observed in related Gerres species, as direct measurements at the moment of eclosion for this taxon remain scarce in the literature. At a sustained temperature of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], the yolk-sac larva relies entirely on endogenous reserves during its first few days of life, undergoing rapid differentiation of the visual and digestive systems before the onset of exogenous feeding. The tiny size of these prolarvae means they are subject to intense predation pressure and high dispersal mortality, a demographic bottleneck that is partially offset by the production of numerous small eggs over repeated spawning events. Following yolk-sac resorption, the free-swimming larva begins to feed on microzooplankton, initiating a period of exponential growth that continues until metamorphosis and eventual settlement into shallow nursery habitats. This early life history strategy is typical of marine teleosts that exploit productive coastal environments for larval development.

Under the thermal conditions prevalent in its natural habitat, namely a water temperature of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], the maximum documented lifespan for Gerres cinereus is equivalent to 5110 days [am = 5110 days], a longevity that places it among the longer-lived members of its genus. This estimate of fourteen years was derived from otolith increment analysis of the oldest individuals recovered from a long-term monitoring program in the waters surrounding the Bahamas archipelago. The benign and seasonally stable thermal regime of the subtropical western Atlantic likely contributes to this extended viability, as metabolic rates remain moderate and cumulative oxidative damage accumulates at a slower pace than in more thermally variable environments. Senescent individuals are rarely captured in fishery surveys, suggesting that natural mortality from predation likely truncates the population age structure well before the physiological maximum is reached. This life history profile aligns with that of other coastal gerreids that occupy stable, food-rich habitats and face moderate predation regimes throughout their adult lives.
